analysis.one_liner: Blocks abusive high-cost mortgage practices like balloon payments, prepayment penalties, and mandatory arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2000, the bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten rules on high-cost home mortgages: lenders would have to verify that borrowers can actually afford the payments from income, not just home equity. It would ban balloon payments, cap and limit prepayment penalties, prohibit single-premium credit insurance folded into loans, cap financed points and fees, bar mandatory arbitration clauses, and raise penalties and the time limit for suing over violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners taking out high-rate or fee-heavy home loans, especially older and lower-income borrowers who often were sold loans they could not repay and risked losing their homes to foreclosure.
analysis.who_pays: High-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers, and credit insurance sellers would lose profitable practices; lenders argued the tighter affordability test would make some borrowers unable to get home loans at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subprime lenders and credit insurance sellers
analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main trade-off is real but narrow: a stricter ability-to-repay rule based only on income could deny credit to some older homeowners whose wealth is mostly their house equity, and higher penalties could raise lender costs that get passed on. The bill targets only the higher-cost segment of the market, so standard prime mortgages would be unaffected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee on April 12, 2000, and the committee, chaired by Sen. Phil Gramm, never acted on it; Congress expired on January 3, 2001, so the bill died with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action of any kind.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers, and credit insurance sellers kept their existing practices because the bill never reached a vote.

for.name: Sen. Paul Sarbanes
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Predatory Lending Consumer Protection Act of 2000 and gave introductory remarks on April 12, 2000.

for.name: Sens. Christopher Dodd, Chuck Schumer, and John Kerry
for.role: U.S. Senators from Connecticut, New York, and Massachusetts
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 12, 2000, and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which kept it from ever reaching the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats; the bill was referred to a Banking Committee whose chair was a Republican and which took no action on it, with no recorded votes on the bill at any stage.

industries.note: The bill bans their most profitable features — balloon payments, large financed fees, single-premium credit insurance, and prepayment penalties after two years — and requires real income-based underwriting. These loans put borrowers' homes at risk of foreclosure.

industries.industry: Credit life and disability insurance sellers
industries.note: The bill bans the advance sale of single-premium credit insurance financed into the loan, a product that added thousands to loan balances for coverage many borrowers never needed.
All broker compensation would count toward the bill's points-and-fees cap, and the bill's limits on financed fees would cut broker payouts on high-cost loans.

industries.industry: Buyers and holders of securitized high-cost mortgages
industries.note: Assignees of home-improvement-related high-cost loans would inherit all the borrower's claims and defenses against the original contractor and lender, making these loans riskier to buy.
